body.heading: Most listening is really waiting
paragraphs: In ordinary conversation, much of our “listening” is privately rehearsing: composing the reply, the similar story, the advice. The other person can usually tell. They may not name it, but they feel the difference between being heard and being waited out.

Mindful listening is the decision to give the speaker the whole of your attention for the length of their sentence — and then the next one. It is simple to describe and surprisingly athletic to do, which is exactly what makes it a practice.

body.heading: The practice, in conversation
paragraphs: Let them finish — the whole thought, including the pause where they are finding the rest of it. Silence after someone speaks is not a failure of the conversation; it is often where the real sentence arrives. Count two beats before responding if you need a tool.

When your mind wanders to your reply, notice and return, the same as any meditation. Ask questions that open rather than steer: “What was that like?” beats “Don’t you think you should…?” almost every time. And when you do speak, try reflecting one thing you heard before adding anything of your own.

body.heading: What it gives both people
paragraphs: The speaker gets the rare experience of being fully received, which tends to make people clearer, calmer and more honest — we think better when we are truly heard. The listener gets a rest from the noise of their own rehearsing, and usually learns something the reply would have trampled.
Start with low stakes: one conversation a day, perhaps with the person easiest to half-listen to out of sheer familiarity. Those are often the conversations where full attention changes the most.

takeaway: Give the speaker the whole sentence, and the pause after it — attention is the gift.
